items.title: Oxford museum displays seized belongings of Naga freedom fighter Gaidinliu for first time
items.desc: Notebooks, clothes and ritual objects taken by British forces in the 1930s go on show at the Pitt Rivers Museum In 1932, British forces in north-east India imprisoned a 17-year-old girl called Gaidinliu for leading an uprising against colonial rule. While pursuing the freedom fighter through hills and valleys in the homeland of the Naga people, colonial officers also seized some of her most treasured possessions. They were sent to the University of Oxford’s Pitt Rivers Museum and kept in storage. Now, for the first time, the museum is exhibiting the collection of 27 items, including a basket of Gaidinliu’s notebooks believed to contain her prophetic visions as the leader of a Naga Indigenous religion, clothes, bracelets and amulets. Continue reading...

items.title: Number of Neets in UK falls below a million as Burnham pushes to tackle crisis

As ministers prepare to make sweeping changes in response to Alan Milburn’s landmark report on young people and work, the Office for National Statistics said the number of Neets fell by 22,000 in the three months to September, to 959,000. items.title: What we learned from the government’s latest release of Mandelson documents
items.desc: From attempted influence on Starmer’s 2025 reshuffle to refusing to sell shares in a lobbying firm, here are some of the key points UK politics live – latest updates The government has published 32 new documents about Peter Mandelson’s appointment and tenure as British ambassador to Washington. This is the third tranche of papers since a parliamentary motion, known as a humble address, in February 2026 for “all papers” relevant to be released. Some material was withheld by the Metropolitan police from earlier releases in March and June on the basis it could prejudice an ongoing investigation into Mandelson. A number of files continue to be withheld but earlier this month the force informed the government that various records could now be disclosed. Continue reading...

The government put what it is calling the “cutting costs bill” before parliament on Thursday, beginning the legislation to put the deal into law after it was agreed with the EU last Friday – though the deal to ease access for food and drink exports will not come into force until 2028, with the emissions trading deal to follow that year. The faulty electrical appliances, including toasters and slow cookers, had been returned to major UK supermarkets. They were found at Agbogbloshie, one of the world’s largest e-waste sites, in Ghana’s capital, Accra, a joint investigation by Unearthed and Greenpeace Africa has found. The findings raise serious questions about e-waste export rules. Continue reading...
